title: Analyzing Graphs of f, f', and f''
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: A function and its derivatives are three views of one object; every feature of one appears as a specific feature of the others.
The height of the graph of f' at a point equals the slope of the graph of f at that point, because f' is the slope of f.
The slope of the graph of f' equals f'', which gives the concavity of f.
Where the f' graph is above the x-axis, f is increasing; where it is below, f is decreasing.
Where the f' graph crosses zero from positive to negative, f has a local maximum; from negative to positive, f has a local minimum.
Where the f' graph is rising (increasing), f is concave up; where it is falling, f is concave down.
Where the f' graph has a local maximum or minimum, f has an inflection point, because f'' changes sign there.
Questions about direction and extrema of f read the height and zeros of f'; questions about concavity and inflection of f read the slope and turning points of f'.
Example: if f' decreases from 2 to −2 on [0, 2] crossing zero at x = 1, then f increases on (0, 1), decreases after, and has a local maximum at x = 1.
In that example, f is concave down on (0, 2) because f' is decreasing, and an inflection point occurs where f' reaches its minimum.
The deadliest error is treating the graph of f' as if it were the graph of f, which reverses conclusions about increase and concavity.
A rising f' graph does NOT mean f is increasing; it means f is concave up, since the increase/decrease of f depends on the sign of f', not its slope.
A maximum point on the f' graph is not a maximum of f; it is an inflection point of f.
To match unlabeled graphs as f, f', and f'', align each derivative's zeros with the previous graph's extrema or horizontal tangents.
The extrema of f' line up with the inflection points of f and with the zeros of f''.
The sine family is a clean anchor: if f = sin x then f' = cos x and f'' = −sin x.
For sin x, the maximum at x = π/2 lines up with cos x crossing zero from positive to negative, matching the rule that a max of f is a downward zero crossing of f'.
Height and overall shape are not reliable for matching graphs; the alignment of zeros with extrema is the dependable check.
On free response with an f' graph, the absolute extrema of f on a closed interval come from the Candidates Test using f' = 0 points and the endpoints.
Conclusions about f from an f' graph must be justified by explicit reference to f', such as 'f' changes from positive to negative.'
Reconstructing f from f' is qualitative here, but the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus later makes it quantitative: net change in f equals the signed area under the f' graph.
Fluency in translating among f, f', and f'' is the conceptual bridge between differentiation, which breaks a function into rate information, and integration, which builds it back up.
